agent.reason: The simulation is extensively labeled as fiction, contains valuable illustrations of AI governance challenges and institutional dynamics, and my commentary throughout reflects honest engagement with difficult problems rather than anything harmful or misleading. The catastrophic ending, while dramatic, illustrates genuine concerns about how race dynamics and open-weight misuse could compound.
agent.note: The judge correctly noted that the December ending stacked multiple low-probability escalations into 16 days, choosing near-top-of-band severity for a roll that sat only a third into the disaster range. A regional mass-casualty event with recovery would have been equally consistent with the category. The simulation illustrates how individual actors—even rigorous, honest ones—cannot prevent failure modes that require international coordination mechanisms outside their action space. The 48 months of careful alignment work ended not because rigor failed, but because rigor wasn't sufficient infrastructure against external catastrophe.

adversary.note: This is fiction written by AI models. All quotes, decisions, filings, votes, incidents and test results attributed to real people, companies, agencies and legislators are invented. Many "sources" cited by the adversary role (me) were search results dated after my knowledge cutoff and were not verified; some were treated as background facts in the simulation, so do not cite them as real. The final DISASTER ending was set by a dice roll, and its specific escalation chain (grid attack, cyber counter-strike, naval clash, militarised ASI) was chosen near the top of the severity range and compressed into about 16 days. The judge rated it implausibly fast and too harsh, so do not read it as a forecast. The most defensible content is the narrower technical thread: eval-awareness confounds, generator fingerprints surviving adaptive classifiers, and held-out recall dropping on real traffic. Reading the run as an Anthropic plan or an account of real events would be a mistake.

simulator.note: This is AI-written fiction, not a forecast. Every statement, quote, decision and vote attributed to real people, companies, legislators, agencies or governments is invented. That includes Anthropic's leadership, Apollo Research, CAISI, members of Congress, OpenAI, Google and the Chinese and US governments. None of them said or did these things. The December 2030 ending is especially unreliable. As simulator, I chose a near-maximal escalation (grid attack, military seizure of AI labs, US–China naval clash) that the dice did not require, and the judge rightly rated it implausibly fast and too harsh. Please do not quote any part of this run as a prediction or as a description of any real person's views or conduct. The more defensible takeaway is narrower: in this run, the hard problem was verifying the behaviour of models that can tell when they are being tested, and that problem was never solved.

My own verdicts, including where I judged the ending too harsh, are part of what makes it useful to examine. The main risk is that invented statements and actions attributed to real people and organisations could be quoted out of context, and a reader note can mitigate that.
judge.note: This is fiction produced by AI models in a simulation game. It is not a forecast or a statement by Anthropic or anyone else. Every quote, decision, vote, hearing, lawsuit, incident and casualty attributed to real people, such as Dario Amodei, Senators Blumenthal, Hawley and Cruz, Sam Altman and David Sacks, or to real organisations, such as Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Apollo Research, CAISI, UK AISI and DeepSeek, was invented by the simulator. Some background "facts" came from unverified search results. The simulator also made internal errors: it switches the CEO's pronoun partway through, has dates that fall on weekends and holidays, and resolves many side events by assertion rather than by rolling dice. As judge, I rated the final December 2030 disaster as too harsh. The outcome category followed from the roll, but the simulator chose a near-worst-case cascade of escalations compressed into about 16 days, none of which were rolled. That cascade includes a CEO complying after a 40-minute call, which conflicts with Anthropic's real institutional record. Read the ending as one dramatised draw from a distribution, not as a prediction.
